blocks.text: OpenAI has two ways for an agent to pick up new abilities, its own native function calling, and MCP.
The Agents SDK lets you mix both in one agent, native functions, built in tools like web search, and whole MCP servers.
This lesson walks through how that wiring actually works, and what to watch for when you combine tool sources.
1. What the OpenAI Agents SDK Is
The Agents SDK is OpenAI's official framework for building agents in Python, replacing the older experimental Swarm project.
An agent in this SDK is just a bundle of instructions, a model, and a list of tools it is allowed to call.
Those tools can be plain Python functions, OpenAI hosted built in tools, or entire MCP servers attached to the agent.
2. Native Function Calling versus MCP Based Tool Calling

blocks.alt: Native Function Calling versus MCP Based Tool Calling
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450711-263907168.png
Native function calling means you write a Python function, decorate or register it, and the SDK builds its schema from the function signature.
MCP based tool calling means the tool logic lives outside your process entirely, inside a separate MCP server the agent connects to.
The model itself cannot tell the difference, both show up as ordinary tools it can call by name with arguments.

blocks.text: 3. Why Wire MCP Into an OpenAI Agent
Once a tool exists as an MCP server, any MCP aware host can use it, not just one hardcoded agent.
That means the same filesystem, database, or ticketing tool can serve a Claude based assistant and an OpenAI agent without duplicating code.

blocks.title: Reuse is the point
blocks.content: MCP moves tool logic out of the agent codebase, so teams stop rewriting the same integration for every model or framework they use.

blocks.text: 4. Installing the Agents SDK
Getting started only needs one package and an API key set as an environment variable.
The package installs both the core Agent and Runner classes and the agents.mcp module used for MCP servers.
No separate MCP client library is needed, the SDK handles the protocol details internally.
5. Wiring a Local MCP Server via Stdio

blocks.alt: Wiring a Local MCP Server via Stdio
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450712-393791634.png
A locally spawned MCP server, one launched as a child process, connects through MCPServerStdio.
You pass it the command and arguments needed to start the server, then hand it to the agent as an mcp_servers entry.

code.content:
import asyncio
from agents import Agent, Runner
from agents.mcp import MCPServerStdio

async def main():
    async with MCPServerStdio(
        name="Filesystem MCP Server",
        params={
            "command": "npx",
            "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/tmp/shared"],
        },
    ) as mcp_server:
        agent = Agent(
            name="File Assistant",
            instructions="Use the filesystem tools to answer questions about the shared folder.",
            mcp_servers=[mcp_server],
        )
        result = await Runner.run(agent, "List the files in the shared folder")
        print(result.final_output)

asyncio.run(main())

blocks.text: The async with block matters, it makes sure the server process starts up and shuts down cleanly around the run.
Forgetting this cleanup step is a common source of orphaned child processes during development.
6. Wiring a Remote MCP Server via HTTP
A server running independently, reachable over the network, connects through MCPServerStreamableHttp instead.
The setup looks almost identical, only the params change from a spawned command to a URL.

code.content:
from agents.mcp import MCPServerStreamableHttp

async def main():
    async with MCPServerStreamableHttp(
        name="Docs MCP Server",
        params={"url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp"},
    ) as mcp_server:
        agent = Agent(
            name="Docs Assistant",
            instructions="Answer questions using the internal documentation tools.",
            mcp_servers=[mcp_server],
        )
        result = await Runner.run(agent, "How do I reset a customer password?")
        print(result.final_output)

blocks.text: 7. How Tool Discovery and Schema Conversion Works
When an agent runs, the SDK calls list_tools on every attached MCP server to learn what it offers.
Each MCP tool schema gets converted into the same function schema format the model expects for native tools.
From the model's point of view there is no separate MCP category, just one flat list of callable tools.
8. Mixing MCP Tools with OpenAI Built in Tools

blocks.alt: Mixing MCP Tools with OpenAI Built in Tools
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450712-463928857.png
A single agent can hold native functions, built in tools such as WebSearchTool, and MCP servers all at once.

code.content:
from agents import Agent, WebSearchTool
from agents.mcp import MCPServerStdio

async def build_agent(mcp_server):
    return Agent(
        name="Research Assistant",
        instructions="Use web search for current events and MCP tools for internal documents.",
        tools=[WebSearchTool()],
        mcp_servers=[mcp_server],
    )

blocks.text: Practical considerations come up quickly once you mix sources this way.

items: Tool names must stay unique across native tools, built in tools, and every attached MCP server.
Latency stacks up, each MCP server adds its own round trip on top of the model call itself.
Built in tools like web search or code interpreter run inside OpenAI, MCP tools run wherever the server lives.
Instructions should tell the model when to prefer one tool source over another, the model cannot guess that on its own.
A failing MCP server should not silently drop tools the agent still thinks it has access to.

blocks.text: 9. Approval Flows for MCP Tool Calls

blocks.alt: Approval Flows for MCP Tool Calls
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450713-70284294.png
Because MCP tools can reach outside your own codebase, the SDK and the Responses API both support requiring approval before a call runs.
Setting require_approval to always pauses the run and hands control back to your code before anything executes.
10. Caching the Tool List
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450714-981337423.png
Calling list_tools on every single run adds a network round trip before the model even sees a prompt.
For a server whose tools rarely change, caching that list avoids paying that cost on every request.

code.content:
mcp_server = MCPServerStdio(
    name="Filesystem MCP Server",
    params={"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/tmp/shared"]},
    cache_tools_list=True,
)

blocks.text: Turn caching off again the moment a server's tools change during development, otherwise the agent keeps using stale definitions.
11. The Responses API MCP Tool Type
Outside the Agents SDK, the plain Responses API also understands MCP directly through a tool of type mcp.

code.content:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    input="What is the current status of ticket 4521?",
    tools=[{
        "type": "mcp",
        "server_label": "support_tools",
        "server_url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
        "require_approval": "never",
    }],
)
print(response.output_text)

blocks.text: This path is useful when you want MCP tool access without adopting the full Agents SDK orchestration layer.
12. Tracing and Observability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450714-335947244.png
The Agents SDK ships built in tracing that records every tool call an agent makes during a run.
MCP tool calls show up in that trace the same way native function calls do, with arguments, results, and timing.
That shared view matters most once an agent mixes several tool sources, otherwise debugging a slow run means guessing which source was slow.
13. Performance and Latency Considerations
Every attached MCP server adds connection setup time, and every tool call adds its own network hop on top of the model call.
An agent with three MCP servers and heavy tool use will feel noticeably slower than one relying only on native functions.
Keeping the number of attached servers small, and caching tool lists where safe, keeps that overhead manageable.
14. Choosing Between Native Functions and MCP

blocks.alt: Choosing Between Native Functions and MCP
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441450715-865310841.png
Native function calling still wins for small, app specific logic that never needs to leave your codebase.
MCP wins once a tool needs to be shared across agents, frameworks, or even different model providers entirely.

blocks.title: A simple rule of thumb
blocks.content: If you would copy paste the same tool code into a second project, that tool probably belongs behind an MCP server instead.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Here is one agent using all three tool sources together, a native function, a built in tool, and an MCP server.
The agent picks whichever tool fits the request without needing to know which category it came from.

code.content:
import asyncio
from agents import Agent, Runner, WebSearchTool, function_tool
from agents.mcp import MCPServerStdio

@function_tool
def internal_ticket_priority(ticket_id: str) -> str:
    """Look up the priority level for an internal ticket id."""
    return "high" if ticket_id.endswith("1") else "normal"

async def main():
    async with MCPServerStdio(
        name="Support MCP Server",
        params={"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "support-mcp-server"]},
        cache_tools_list=True,
    ) as mcp_server:
        agent = Agent(
            name="Support Assistant",
            instructions=(
                "Use internal_ticket_priority for priority questions, "
                "web search for anything about current outages, "
                "and the MCP tools for ticket details."
            ),
            tools=[WebSearchTool(), internal_ticket_priority],
            mcp_servers=[mcp_server],
        )
        result = await Runner.run(agent, "Is ticket 4521 high priority, and any active outages?")
        print(result.final_output)

asyncio.run(main())

blocks.text: Common Mistakes

items: Attaching an MCP server without an async with block, leaving the server process running or shutting down uncleanly.
Giving a native function and an MCP tool the same name, so the model cannot reliably tell them apart.
Leaving cache_tools_list on while actively editing an MCP server, then wondering why new tools never appear.
Forgetting that built in tools run inside OpenAI while MCP tools run wherever the server is hosted, and assuming both share one environment.
Skipping require_approval on an MCP server that can perform destructive actions like deletes.
Writing instructions that never mention which tool source to prefer, leaving the choice entirely up to the model.

blocks.text: Practice
Take the filesystem MCP server from section 5 and add a native function_tool that formats file sizes in a friendly way.
Attach both tools to one agent, and write instructions telling it to format any size it reports using the new function.
Confirm in the trace output that both tool sources were actually called during the same run.
Key Takeaway
OpenAI agents can call native functions, hosted built in tools, and MCP servers side by side, all as one merged tool list.
Reach for MCP when a tool needs to be shared beyond one agent, and keep native functions for small logic that stays local.
Hosted built in tools remain the right pick whenever OpenAI already manages the entire capability end to end.
